title: Psalm 82: God Judges the Judges
summary: God takes his place in a heavenly assembly and puts the powers who rule the world on trial. He charges them with judging unjustly and favoring the wicked, commands them to defend the weak, the fatherless, and the oppressed, and sentences them to die like mortals. The psalmist then calls on God himself to rise and judge the earth, because all the nations belong to him.
story: Psalm 82 sits in the Asaph collection (Psalms 73 to 83) near the middle of Book III of the Psalter, the book that wrestles most openly with the collapse of Israel's security: a ruined sanctuary in Psalm 74, a people in distress in Psalms 79 and 80, and finally the fallen house of David in Psalm 89. Psalm 81 had God pleading with Israel to listen to him. Psalm 82 widens the frame to the whole world. The trouble is no longer only Israel's disobedience but the corruption of every power that governs the nations. The psalm's answer is that God has not abandoned the world to them. He sits as judge over the judges, and the closing prayer asks him to take back direct rule of the earth. That longing, for God himself to set the world right, is one of the threads the rest of the Bible pulls forward.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to Asaph. According to Chronicles, Asaph was one of the Levite musicians David appointed to lead worship (1 Chronicles 16:4-5), and his descendants continued as a guild of temple singers long afterward, some returning from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:41). A psalm “of Asaph” may therefore come from Asaph himself or from the singers who carried his name. The headings are ancient, but whether they were part of the original compositions or added by later editors is debated. Some scholars read them as reliable notes of authorship; others take them as marks of the collection a psalm came from.

Nothing in Psalm 82 names an event or a king. Its concern with unjust rulers who ignore the poor fits any period of Israel's monarchy, and it echoes the charges of eighth-century prophets such as Amos and Isaiah against judges who took bribes and ignored widows and orphans. Some scholars date it early because it uses the old picture of a divine council; others date it late because it announces the death of every rival power. The text itself gives no firm clue, and it has been prayed in every century since as a protest against corrupt authority.
cultural:
The ancient Near East pictured the heavens as a royal court. Texts from the Canaanite city of Ugarit (thirteenth century BC) describe the high god El presiding over an assembly of gods, the sons of El. Israel's Scriptures use similar language for the beings who surround God's throne: the host of heaven in Micaiah's vision (1 Kings 22:19), the sons of God who present themselves before the LORD in Job 1 and 2, and the heavenly beings of Psalm 89. In Deuteronomy 32:8, the nations were apportioned “according to the number of the sons of God” (the BSB here follows a Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript and the Greek; the traditional Hebrew text reads sons of Israel), which many read as the idea that other nations were placed under lesser heavenly powers while Israel remained the LORD's own portion. Psalm 82 stages a trial in that court, and in it the God of Israel is not one member among many but the judge of all.

The duties God demands are the standard duties of a just king in the ancient world. Mesopotamian law collections, including Hammurabi's (eighteenth century BC), present the ruler as the one who protects the widow and the orphan from the strong. The fatherless, the poor, and the afflicted were the people with no male protector, no land, and no voice at the city gate where cases were heard. A judge who favored the wealthy left them with no recourse at all. The psalm measures every power, human or heavenly, by what it does for them.
literary: The psalm is built like a courtroom scene. Verse 1 is narration that sets the scene: God “presides in the divine assembly”. Verses 2 to 7 are God's own speech, the charge (verse 2), the commands the accused have failed to keep (verses 3 and 4), the verdict on their blindness and its cosmic result (verse 5), and the sentence (verses 6 and 7). Verse 8 steps out of the scene into prayer, as the worshiper asks God to do on earth what he has just declared in heaven. The word judge frames the whole poem: God judges in verse 1, the accused judge unjustly in verse 2, and the psalmist asks God to judge the earth in verse 8. The sentence turns on a sharp contrast: “You are gods” set against “like mortals you will die”. The shaking of “all the foundations of the earth” in verse 5 shows that injustice is not a private failing; it unsettles the order of the world.

outline.t: God takes his seat in the divine assembly
The charge: unjust judgment and neglect of the weak
The accused walk in darkness and the earth shakes
The sentence: the gods will die like mortals
The prayer: rise, O God, and judge the earth

doctrines.note: God is the judge of every power in heaven and on earth, and he holds rulers accountable above all for how they treat the weak. The psalm ends by longing for that judgment, because for the oppressed God's judgment is good news.
Whatever powers govern the nations, they govern under God and answer to him. “All the nations are Your inheritance” (verse 8): no people or territory lies outside his claim.
God's holiness is not remote. In this psalm it takes the shape of justice for the fatherless and the afflicted, and it condemns any authority that bends judgment toward the powerful.

words.note: Elohim, here gods. The same Hebrew word normally means God (as in verse 1's first line) but can also refer to plural divine or heavenly beings, and in a few passages it is used of human judges acting in God's name (compare Exodus 21:6 and 22:8, where some translations render it judges). Which sense applies in verses 1 and 6 is the central question of the psalm, set out below.

Edah, congregation or assembly. It is the usual word for the gathered community of Israel in the wilderness. Here it describes the assembly that surrounds God (literally the assembly of El), which is why the BSB renders it “the divine assembly”.

Shaphat, to judge. The verb covers more than handing down verdicts; it means to govern, to rule, and to put things right, especially for those who have been wronged. It appears four times in eight verses, and the whole psalm turns on who judges and how.

christ: Jesus quoted this psalm when he was accused of blasphemy for calling himself God's Son: “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I have said you are gods’?” (John 10:34). His argument runs from lesser to greater. If Scripture could call them gods to whom God's word came, how much more can the one the Father sanctified and sent into the world call himself the Son of God (John 10:35-36). The psalm also sets up a longing that the New Testament says is answered in him. Verse 8 asks God to rise and judge the earth and claim the nations as his inheritance, and the New Testament presents the risen Jesus as the one appointed to judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31) and the one to whom the nations are given. Where the unjust powers of Psalm 82 failed the weak and fatherless, Jesus announced good news to the poor and was himself condemned by a corrupt court. The connection is not a prediction hidden in the psalm but a hope the psalm voices and the gospel claims is fulfilled.

hard.q: Who are the gods whom God judges, and does the psalm mean there are other gods?
hard.a:
Interpreters give three main answers. The first reads the gods as human rulers and judges. Their task was to judge in God's name, so they bore a divine title, and the charges (partiality, neglect of the poor) are exactly the sins of earthly courts. Jesus' use of the psalm in John 10 is often read this way, since he speaks of those to whom the word of God came. The second reads them as heavenly beings, members of God's council who were given oversight of the nations (compare Deuteronomy 32:8) and who have ruled them badly. This view points to the setting in verse 1, the sentence that they will die like mortals (which is only surprising if they are not mortals), and the parallel scenes in 1 Kings 22 and Job 1. The third, found in ancient Jewish interpretation, reads the gods as Israel at Sinai, given God's word and a share of immortality they lost through sin.

None of these views requires the psalm to teach that there are other gods equal to the LORD. Even on the second reading, the other powers are created beings under his authority, and the psalm's whole point is that they are answerable to him and will fall. The Old Testament can call such beings elohim while confessing that the LORD alone is God. Readers who hold the same faith differ on which reading is best, and each can account for Jesus' argument in John 10.

questions: The psalm judges every power by what it does for the weak and fatherless. Who in your community has no one to defend their cause, and who is supposed to?
Verse 5 says injustice shakes the foundations of the earth. Why might the Bible treat corruption in courts and governments as a matter of cosmic importance rather than only politics?
The psalm ends by asking God to judge the earth. When have you wanted God's judgment, and when have you feared it?
